extracted.intended_audience: Citizens/voters (specifically the people of New York) and the general literate public engaged in the ratification debate
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for citizens and commentators on how to judge and defend (or object to) the proposed federal Constitution — weighing its defects, comparing it to the Articles of Confederation, and determining whether it is republican in form. Emphasizes standards for fair criticism, practical comparison, and the essential qualities of a republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from predetermined bias in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not approach the plan 'with a predisposition to censure' or with a 'predetermination to condemn'; opinions formed from such biases are of little value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between 'predetermined patron' (whose bias may be from sincere motives) and 'predetermined adversary' (whose views are culpable). The papers are addressed to those who 'add to a sincere zeal for the happiness of their country, a temper favorable to a just estimate of the means of promoting it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for human fallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that a faultless plan was not to be expected and make allowances for errors attributable to the fallibility of those who framed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should also remember their own fallibility and not assume infallibility when rejudging others' opinions; allowances ought to be made for difficulties inherent in the undertaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to novelty and lack of precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the undertaking is novel and past confederacies are vitiated by erroneous principles, one should not expect perfect precedent-guidance and must accept the need for new arrangements and future correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past confederacies can serve as beacons warning what to avoid but cannot point clearly to what must be pursued; the convention could at most avoid past errors and provide means to rectify future discovered errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance stability and energy with republican liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution must combine requisite stability and energy in government with 'inviolable attention due to liberty and to the republican form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energy is essential for security and law execution; stability is essential for national character and public confidence. But republican genius demands that power derive from the people, be held by many hands, and often for short tenures — creating tension between stability (longer tenure, continuity) and republican rotation/short duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful partition of federal and State authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Partitioning authority between the general (federal) and State governments is inherently difficult and requires moderation of expectations about precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies to difficulty of defining faculties or legal jurisdictions: boundaries are delicate and often indeterminate, so imprecision in partition should be expected and settled pragmatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept compromises arising from conflicting interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Compromises between large and small states, and among local interests, are inevitable; theoretical symmetry must often yield to extraneous considerations to form an operative union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because states differ in wealth, size, and local policy interests, neither side (large or small) would fully yield; hence compromise and sacrifice of theoretical propriety were likely and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary multiplication of constitutional experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lightly subject the government to repeated experiments or frequent remaking by successive conventions; stability in the system is preferable unless a clearly better alternative is agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples show many reforms were done by single lawgivers rather than assemblies; ad hoc or repeated overhauls risk discord and instability. If a second convention is proposed, expect similar discord and uncertain improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical superiority over existing system is sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed constitution need not be perfect; it is sufficient that it be an improvement over the current Confederation ('the latter is more imperfect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pragmatic comparison: one should accept a better, though imperfect, system rather than retain a clearly worse one (analogy: trading a shattered habitation for a firmer building despite imperfections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require coherent alternatives from objectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics opposing the proposed remedy should present an agreed-upon alternative; if objectors cannot agree among themselves, their objections carry less weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those who object cannot propose a consistent substitute (or disagree among themselves), prudence favors following the unanimous recommendation of the capable counsellors who proposed the remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare objections to the new plan with defects of the Confederation
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating objections to the new Constitution, check whether similar or worse defects exist in the Articles of Confederation; many objections apply equally or more strongly to the existing system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lists examples: indefinite federal powers to raise money or troops, mixing powers in one body, absence of a bill of rights, treaty-making power, and permitting importation of slaves — noting Confederation already exhibits many dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of effective powers commensurate to objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A government must possess regular, effective powers proportional to its responsibilities; otherwise it is driven to overleap constitutional limits or becomes impotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Confederation declared powers necessary but rendered them nugatory; lack of proper powers leads to either assumption of power or dissolution/usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware concentration of independent funds and military power
rubrics_metrics.description: The transfer of large independent resources (e.g., western lands) and the ability to raise troops by a single body without constitutional authority is dangerously concentrating power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress's administration of western territories, formation of governments, and appointment of officers 'without the least color of constitutional authority' is cited as alarming; argues for structuring powers to avoid unchecked concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'republic' — source and tenure of power
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding office during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential that power be derived from the great body of society (not from a favored class). It is sufficient that officers be appointed directly or indirectly by the people and that tenures be one of the specified types; examples: most State constitutions appoint chief magistrates indirectly and fix definite tenures, while judiciary often hold by good behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and essentiality tests for republican character
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether a government is republican: essential—powers must derive from the great body of the people; sufficient—officers appointed (directly/indirectly) by the people and holding office by limited tenures or good behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses comparative examples (Holland, Venice, Poland, England) to show misuse of the term 'republic' and to motivate the proposed definitional criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of language and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspicuity requires distinct ideas and appropriate words; complexity and novelty of objects make definitions unavoidably inexact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three sources of vagueness: indistinctness of the object, imperfection of the cognitive organ, and inadequacy of language; these enlarge difficulty in delineating jurisdictions and constitutional provisions.
